title: Build a personal two-pattern error log
instructions: Use Tika's eight dated review entries: (1) 2 October, composition—wrote ‘The bus was late, we missed the first talk’; feedback identified two complete clauses joined only by a comma. (2) 4 October, composition—wrote ‘The poll proves every student wants a longer break’ although 15 of 24 students voted for it. (3) 7 October, vocabulary—chose ‘jubilant’ for a neutral school report because the rarer word seemed better. (4) 10 October, composition—wrote ‘Our stall sold out, we raised money for the library’; feedback again identified two complete clauses joined only by a comma. (5) 13 October, open cloze—used one wrong preposition in a fixed phrase. (6) 16 October, composition—wrote ‘This method always works’ after describing one three-day test. (7) 21 October, grammar—wrote ‘The box of books were heavy’ and then changed ‘were’ to ‘was’ herself by finding the main noun of the subject. (8) 24 October, composition—wrote ‘The rain stopped, we walked to the field’; feedback again identified two complete clauses joined only by a comma. Answer all six questions before viewing feedback.

parts.prompt: Which THREE entries show one repeated sentence-boundary pattern?

options.text: Entry 1: ‘The bus was late, we missed the first talk.’
Entry 3: choosing ‘jubilant’ for a neutral report
Entry 4: ‘Our stall sold out, we raised money for the library.’
Entry 7: ‘The box of books were heavy.’
Entry 8: ‘The rain stopped, we walked to the field.’

choice_rationales.A: Two complete clauses are joined only by a comma.
choice_rationales.B: This is a word-choice problem, not a sentence boundary.
choice_rationales.C: The same pattern appears again on a later date.
choice_rationales.D: This is an agreement error, and Tika fixed it herself.
choice_rationales.E: The same pattern appears a third time.

parts.hint: Look for the same structure repeated, not just any entry with a grammar error.
parts.correct_explanation: Entries 1, 4 and 8 show the same choice on three dates: joining complete clauses with only a comma.

parts.prompt: Which label names that repeated pattern most precisely?

options.text: I am careless with punctuation in long sentences.
I join two complete clauses with only a comma.
My English is weak.
I should write shorter compositions.

choice_rationales.A: It is vague, and the three sentences are short.
choice_rationales.B: It names a choice that anyone could spot in a new sentence.
choice_rationales.C: It describes a person, not a pattern that can be checked.
choice_rationales.D: Length is not the problem in these entries.

parts.hint: Choose a label that someone else could use to spot the pattern in a new sentence.
parts.correct_explanation: A precise label names the visible choice rather than a vague personal weakness.

parts.prompt: Which should be Tika's SECOND active pattern alongside the comma splice?

options.text: Claims that go beyond the evidence, shown in entries 2 and 6
Every spelling rule in English, although no spelling error appears in the log
The one wrong preposition in entry 5, because every single error must become an active pattern
Subject–verb agreement, ignoring that entry 7 was a single error Tika corrected herself

choice_rationales.A: Two entries show it, and it changes whether her conclusions are true.
choice_rationales.B: There is no evidence for this in the log.
choice_rationales.C: One slip is not yet a pattern.
choice_rationales.D: It happened once, and she already fixed it herself.

parts.hint: Weigh how often a pattern appears and how much harm it does, and choose one shown in more than one entry.
parts.correct_explanation: Entries 2 and 6 both stretch limited evidence into claims about everyone or always, which damages accuracy.

parts.prompt: Which checking routine best targets Tika's comma-splice pattern?

options.text: Circle every long word and replace it with a rarer synonym.
At each comma, ask if both sides could be complete sentences; if so, use a full stop, semicolon or joining word, then reread.
Delete every comma from the whole composition, so that no comma splice can ever appear anywhere in any of the sentences that she writes.
Write ‘be more careful with commas’ beside each comma splice, then move on without making any fresh attempt at all.

choice_rationales.A: This does nothing about sentence boundaries.
choice_rationales.B: It tells Tika what to notice, what to ask and how to fix it.
choice_rationales.C: Many commas are correct, and removing them all creates new errors.
choice_rationales.D: A reminder with no test or new attempt does not change the habit.

parts.hint: The routine should say what to notice, what question to ask and how to fix it.
parts.correct_explanation: A short clause test turns the logged pattern into an action Tika can repeat on a new sentence.

parts.prompt: Which check best targets the pattern of claims that go beyond the evidence?

options.text: Underline every adjective, even when it does not affect the claim.
Look for words such as every, always, never and proves; compare each claim with what was measured, then narrow any claim that goes further.
Add ‘definitely’ before each conclusion to make it sound certain.
Avoid reporting any result, number or comparison at all, so that no conclusion about the test can ever be questioned or challenged by a reader.

choice_rationales.A: Most adjectives have nothing to do with the claim's strength.
choice_rationales.B: It uses clear trigger words and compares each claim with the evidence.
choice_rationales.C: This makes the claims even stronger.
choice_rationales.D: Leaving out evidence makes the composition weaker, not more accurate.

parts.hint: Use visible trigger words, then compare the claim with the limits of the evidence.
parts.correct_explanation: The scope check catches words like ‘always’ and narrows the claim to what was observed.

parts.prompt: Which one-week plan would make Tika's error log most useful?

options.text: Copy all eight corrected answers once, mark every pattern as solved and throw away the dates.

Keep comma splices and over-strong claims as the two active patterns; attach the clause test and the evidence check; write fresh compositions and do new cloze items; record whether each error was avoided, caught when checking or found only after feedback; then look at several later attempts before dropping either pattern.
Track every possible English error at once and use ‘try harder’ as the routine for each.

Practise only the single preposition from entry 5, because the most recent-looking word-level error should replace all repeated patterns; copy that one corrected sentence ten times, mark both comma splices and over-strong claims as solved, stop recording dates and skip any fresh composition practice for the rest of the week.

choice_rationales.A: Copying shows nothing about new writing, and the dates are needed to track progress.
choice_rationales.B: Two priorities, specific checks, fresh practice and evidence over time make the log useful.
choice_rationales.C: Too many targets and no real routine.
choice_rationales.D: It drops the repeated, high-impact patterns for a one-off slip and stops collecting evidence.

parts.hint: Choose the plan with two priorities, specific checks, fresh practice and evidence collected over time.
parts.correct_explanation: A personal error log chooses a small, evidence-based target, guides practice and needs success on new work before a pattern is dropped.
